text: Crops in the district south of Swift Current are reported a total failure, no rain having fallen since seeding. Many settlers are said to be preparing to leave for the north. July 1914. The grass on the open range is dried up, and ranchers are moving their stock to the river flats. Merchants in town report that few accounts are being paid.
label: drought

text: OTTAWA, June 28, 1921. — Three deaths from heat prostration were reported in the city yesterday, when the thermometer stood at 96 in the shade for the third day in succession. Two of the victims were labourers working on the street railway. Horses dropped in harness on Rideau Street, and the bathing beaches along the river were crowded until long after dark. Ice dealers report that their supplies will be exhausted within the week if the heat continues, and the health department has asked that ice be reserved for families with infants and the sick. Several factories closed at noon, and the government departments released their clerks an hour early.
label: drought

text: Wells are running dry throughout Kings County, N.S., and farmers have been hauling water from the river in puncheons for their stock since the middle of August, 1908. The apple crop is small and the potatoes have scarcely set. Several farmers have been obliged to drive their cattle two and three miles daily to water, and the mill at the falls has been idle for want of a head of water.
label: drought

text: The diary of a homesteader near Bow Island, 1918. "May 30. Wind all day again, no rain. The wheat is up but yellowing. June 22. Hot. Two inches of the field blown into the fence line. Sold the second team. July 15. Nothing to cut. Grasshoppers have taken what the sun left. Mary wants to go back to Ontario. August 1. Neighbour Olsen has loaded his wagons and gone north to the Peace. That makes eleven from this township." The family left the homestead the following spring. The quarter section was later taken over by a neighbour for pasture.
label: drought

text: A dust storm of unusual violence swept the country around Rosetown on May 11, 1926. For the better part of the day the sun was hidden and lamps had to be lit in the houses. Soil from the summer-fallow was piled in drifts along the fence lines and seed was blown clean out of the ground over hundreds of acres. Farmers say the land has not had a good soaking for two years. Several motorists were stranded on the road to Saskatoon when the drifting soil hid the ditches, and the train from the south arrived four hours late.
label: drought

text: Pastures in Bruce County are burned brown and many farmers have begun to feed their winter hay. August 1921.
label: drought

text: Relief is being organized for settlers in the dried-out districts of southeastern Alberta. The Department of Agriculture announced on October 4, 1919, that cars of fodder and seed grain will be shipped at reduced rates, and that families without means will receive coal and flour through the winter. In some townships not one farm in five harvested enough grain to pay for the seed. Municipal councils report that many families have already left, and that those who remain have sold all but one team. School districts in the dry belt have asked for help to keep their schools open, since the farmers cannot pay their taxes.
label: drought

text: The fruit growers of the Okanagan are suffering severely for want of irrigation water. The creeks that feed the ditches have shrunk to a trickle after a winter of light snow and a dry spring, and in some orchards the young trees are dying. July 1925. The irrigation district has cut deliveries to two days a week, and growers are carting water in barrels to save their youngest plantings.
label: drought

text: BRANDON, July 16, 1925. The heat wave which has gripped western Manitoba for a week reached its height yesterday when 104 degrees was recorded at the Experimental Farm. Two harvest hands collapsed in the fields and one has since died. Grain that was promising a fortnight ago is now ripening prematurely and the yield will be light. The heat has also told on livestock: farmers report horses dying in harness, and pasture so scorched that milk cows are being fed hay in midsummer. The Assiniboine is lower than it has been in years, and several towns along the railway have begun hauling water in tank cars for their reservoirs.
label: drought

text: Drought and grasshoppers. Reports from forty points in southern Saskatchewan show the wheat crop for 1920 the poorest in a decade. Where the sun did not burn the grain, the hoppers ate it. In the Weyburn district many farmers did not bother to cut, and turned their cattle into the fields instead. Merchants and implement dealers are carrying the farmers until next year.
label: drought

text: A special train of feed and seed grain left Calgary for the dry belt on March 2, 1922. It carried 38 cars, the gift of farmers in the northern districts.
label: drought

text: Heat in Montreal. Six infants died from the effects of the heat in the poorer wards of the city during the week ending July 10, 1912, according to the medical officer of health, who urged mothers to boil milk and keep babies in the shade. Temperatures exceeded 90 degrees on five successive days, and the park fountains were kept running through the night. The medical officer added that the poorest families, crowded into rear tenements without ventilation, suffer most, and that the free milk depots have been asked to stay open through the evening. Several cases of sunstroke were treated at the General Hospital, two of them labourers on the harbour works.
label: drought

text: The dry spell in Prince Edward Island has now lasted seven weeks. Hay is less than half a crop, the turnips have failed and the streams are lower than anyone remembers. August 1930. Farmers are hauling water for their cattle from the brooks that still run, and in some districts the women are carrying it to the houses by the pailful. Fires have broken out in several woodlots.
label: drought

text: An old-timer from the Hanna district recalled the summer of 1924 for a local history book: "The sky was white with heat from June on. You could walk across the slough where we used to water the horses and not wet your boots. Dad dug three wells that summer and found nothing but sand. By August the Russian thistle was the only green thing on the place, and we cut it for feed. Half the families on our road went away that fall, some to the Peace River and some back to the States."
label: drought

text: The Department of the Interior reports that the dry conditions which prevailed through the spring and summer of 1910 in the region west of Moose Jaw resulted in the failure of crops on about 300 homesteads. Relief in the form of seed and feed has been arranged. Many of the settlers affected came to the district only two years ago.
label: drought

text: Soil drifting. Strong winds on April 29 and 30, 1932, lifted the topsoil from thousands of acres of dry, unprotected fields between Kindersley and the Alberta boundary. Roads were blocked by drifts of fine earth, trains ran late and seeded fields will have to be sown again. Some farmers have begun listing their fields to hold the soil.
label: drought

text: Water shortage in Saint John, N.B. City council has ordered the lawn sprinklers shut off and asked householders to save every drop, the lakes that supply the city being at their lowest level since the waterworks were built. September 1914. Firemen have been warned that pressure may be insufficient on the upper streets.
label: drought

text: Three weeks of blazing heat have parched the market gardens around Winnipeg and sent vegetable prices soaring. July 1916.
label: drought

text: Dry weather throughout Ontario during June and July 1933 has reduced the hay crop by one-third. Many dairy herds are on short rations, and milk shipments to the cities have fallen. Pastures in the eastern counties are bare, and some farmers are cutting green oats to feed their stock. The cheese factories report the poorest July make in years.
label: drought

text: KAMSACK, Sask., August 1928. The worst hot wind in local memory blew for two days, withering the wheat in the head. Farmers report yields as low as four bushels to the acre. The hot wind came out of the southwest on the 5th with the temperature at 101 in the shade, and by the evening of the 6th whole fields that had promised 25 bushels were white and shrivelled. Some farmers have already turned their cattle in to graze.
label: drought

text: The drought of 1949 hit the mixed farms of central Alberta hardest in July, when four weeks passed without measurable rain and the temperature climbed above 90 degrees on twelve days. Hay was scarce and dear, and many farmers shipped cattle to market early rather than winter them. Dugouts went dry, and the municipality hired a water truck to supply families whose wells had failed. Many farmers said it was the driest summer since they came to the district. Gardens failed outright, and the cream cheques that kept families going were cut nearly in half as cows went dry on the scorched pasture.
label: drought

text: Weather Bureau note, Toronto, July 1959: the heat wave of the past week produced the warmest July night on record at the downtown station and is blamed for 23 deaths in the city, most of them among the elderly. Hospitals reported many cases of heat exhaustion. The overnight low did not fall below 76 degrees for three nights.
label: drought

text: PFRA crews dug 1,100 new dugouts in southern Saskatchewan during the 1958 season, as a second dry year drained the sloughs and creeks farmers rely on for stock water.
label: drought

text: The St. Lawrence fell to its lowest level in many years during the dry autumn of 1964, forcing ships to lighten their loads and leaving docks at several river ports high and dry. Farmers in the Eastern Townships hauled water to their herds for weeks. Some townships asked the province for help with water hauling.
label: drought

text: A three-day heat wave, June 1953: Windsor 99°F, London 97°F; four deaths, two by drowning while seeking relief in the lakes.
label: drought

text: Prairie crops have suffered severe drought damage. The provincial crop report of July 20, 1967, said wheat in the west-central districts was heading out at less than a foot tall, and pastures in the southwest were fully dried out. Some farmers were baling cereal crops for feed rather than waiting for a harvest. Dugouts are drying up, and some ranchers are hauling water to cattle from town wells. The report noted that a few timely rains in the northeast had produced fair crops there, but that in a broad belt from Kindersley to the Alberta border the hay crop was the poorest in twenty years, and feed would be in short supply going into the winter.
label: drought

text: In the summer of 1970 the southern part of the Okanagan went 71 days without rain. Orchardists put in emergency wells, and the town of Oliver rationed water to two hours of sprinkling every second day. Apples were small but sweet. Wells dropped by several feet. Range fires were frequent in the hills above the lake.
label: drought

text: Cattle are being shipped out of the Cariboo by the trainload because the range is too dry to carry them through the winter, ranchers said this week. A long spell without rain, followed by a plague of grasshoppers, has left the grasslands bare. (September 1966) Some of the older ranchers say it is the worst they have seen since homesteading days.
label: drought

text: Heat wave, Vancouver, July 1951. A strong ridge of high pressure brought the city its hottest week in fifty years. Beaches were packed by day and some people slept in the parks at night. A woman of 81 and a man of 74 died of heat stroke in rooming houses downtown. Ice and electric fans sold out within two days, and the city's water consumption broke all records. Forestry officials closed the woods on the North Shore mountains because of the extreme fire hazard.
label: drought

text: Dry weather has hurt the potato crop in New Brunswick's upper Saint John valley; growers estimate losses of 25 to 40 per cent. August 1957.
label: drought

text: There was no snow to speak of on the prairie the winter of 1944-45, and the spring was windy and dry. By June the dust was blowing off the fallow on every windy day, and some of the boys at school had to wear wet cloths over their faces walking home. The wheat came up thin and never filled out. Dad said that was the only year he didn't haul a single load to the elevator, and we got through the winter on cream cheques and the rabbits we snared.
label: drought

text: Two summers of scant rainfall and high evaporation have drawn the upper Great Lakes down to levels not seen in decades. By August 1963 cottagers on Georgian Bay were walking out to their boats over dry rock, municipal water intakes at several towns had to be extended, and lake freighters were sailing with reduced loads to clear the shallows. Hydro-electric output at Niagara was reduced, and farmers in the lake counties reported pasture burned brown since June. Weather officials said precipitation over the basin had been below normal in twenty of the past twenty-four months.
label: drought

text: The drought of 1975 in southwestern Ontario: rainfall in June and July was less than one-third of normal across Kent, Essex and Lambton counties. Corn and soybean yields fell sharply and tobacco growers irrigated around the clock. Several townships banned lawn watering. Some dairy farmers began feeding winter silage in August.
label: drought

text: Saskatoon swelters. The city recorded 100 degrees on July 5, 1947, and two men collapsed while working on a construction site. The swimming pools were kept open until the staff themselves were exhausted. The river was crowded with bathers, and the city's water consumption reached a record 11 million gallons. One elderly woman died of heat stroke in her home.
label: drought

text: Hot, dry weather in the Peace River country during July 1973 cut the rapeseed crop sharply. Some fields were plowed down. The provincial government announced emergency hay assistance for livestock producers. Temperatures above 90 degrees on eight days during flowering caused heavy blossom blast, and rainfall at Grande Prairie was less than a third of normal for the month.
label: drought

text: PRAIRIE DUST BLOWS AGAIN. Strong winds on May 4, 1955, raised a black blizzard over the Regina plains that cut visibility to a few hundred feet and halted traffic on No. 1 Highway. Farmers said the soil had been bone-dry since a snow-free winter. Several seeded fields lost their topsoil to a depth of two inches.
label: drought

text: Heat wave, Halifax, August 1966: temperature reached 93°F, the highest in the city in many years. Dozens of people were treated for heat exhaustion at the Victoria General, and the fire department responded to numerous grass fires on the outskirts. The city's ice plants ran around the clock, and the beaches on the Northwest Arm were so crowded that police were called to direct traffic.
label: drought

text: Environment Canada heat warning, Montreal, July 2, 1994: humidex values of 40 to 45 expected today and Sunday. The public health department reported 11 heat-related deaths over the following week, mostly among elderly people living alone in apartments without air conditioning. Cooling centres were opened in community centres and shopping malls. The city also extended hours at public pools.
label: drought

text: Agriculture Canada drought assessment, August 1976: southern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan received less than 40 per cent of normal growing-season rainfall. Average yields for spring wheat are estimated at 14 bushels per acre. Tame hay production is down by half and many producers are reducing herd sizes. Federal and provincial governments have announced a joint feed transportation assistance program. Pasture conditions are poor to very poor across the region, and dugout water supplies are critically low, with algae problems reported. Producers are advised to test water quality before allowing livestock access, and to consider early weaning of calves to reduce pressure on remaining forage.
label: drought

text: Water restrictions were declared in Kelowna on July 21, 1998, after a long period of hot, dry weather drove reservoir levels sharply lower. Lawn watering was limited to evenings on alternate days. Orchardists in the surrounding irrigation districts were asked to water at night, and the fire department warned that hillside grass was tinder-dry.
label: drought
